Borders in the Post-Soviet Region: Unfinished Business? | ISPI

 Commentary 12 Nov 2024

# Borders in the Post-Soviet Region: Unfinished Business? 

 Since the USSR's collapse, ethnic tensions have fueled border conflicts and unrecognized states, destabilizing Eastern Europe and the Caucasus. 

- Commentary Russia, Caucasus and Central Asia 

by Eleonora Tafuro Ambrosetti and Mattia Massoletti

 

Territorial revisions and conflicts following the collapse of the URSS in 1991 provoked increasingly contested spaces and borders. Even prior to its ultimate collapse, as Moscow’s central authority weakened, nationalisms and ethnic contrasts, previously suppressed by the common Soviet identity, began to resurface. In some of the 15 newly independent States, these tensions manifested in the form of territorial disputes and conflicts, resulting in the creation of several de facto states, i.e. separatist entities which are not recognised as sovereign states by the international community. Such entities are South Ossetia and Abkhazia in Georgia, Transnistria in Moldova, and more recently the so-called “People’s republics” of Luhansk and Donetsk in Ukraine. The republic of Nagorno-Karabakh, Artsakh in Armenian, existed between 1991 and 2023, when Azerbaijan retook manu militari full control of the former de facto state prompting an exodus of over 100,000 ethnic Armenian refugees. Recent events in Ukraine and the South Caucasus show that this process is ongoing: military and political tensions, including over shared history, complicate an already challenging situation, and further destabilise borders. 

## The role of Russia 

In a way, the USSR collapse – labelled as the “ major geopolitical disaster of the century” by Vladimir Putin in 2005 – also presented Russia with opportunities to reassert its influence in the region. 

The element of separatism has played an important role in this process. The Russian Federation has both been a victim and a culprit of separatism. If on the one hand it has harshly suppressed the main independentist ambitions within its borders – i.e., those of the republic of Chechnya following the second Chechen war (1999-2007) – on the other, Moscow has stirred separatism in other sovereign countries, fomenting instability to maintain influence. This tactic became part of the Kremlin’s playbook in the early post-Soviet years. Between 1992 and 1994, Russia got involved in several secessionist wars in the ‘near abroad’: in Moldova, it sent a military contingent to aid the separatist forces of Transnistria; in Georgia, it backed the breakaway regions of Abkhazia and South Ossetia; finally, it supported Armenia in its conflict against Azerbaijan over Nagorno-Karabakh. 

All these conflicts have persisted to the present day, with Russia occasionally resorting to military force to support de facto entities – as in Abkhazia and South Ossetia in the context of 2008 Russo-Georgian war. Moscow, however, did not limit itself to meddling in these “first generation” secessionist conflicts: besides annexing Crimea, in 2014, Russia fueled separatist aspirations in the Ukrainian eastern region of Donbas, providing support to the “People’s republics” of Donetsk and Luhansk – and thus laying the foundations for the current full-scale war against Ukraine. 

Beyond providing financial and political support, the Russian leadership has not adopted a universal approach to either secessionist conflicts or to the de facto states in the former USSR area. For example, while it has recognised both Abkhazia and South Ossetia, Moscow has not done the same with Transnistria. Moreover, the Kremlin’s policy has evolved over time – f.i., it was repeatedly stated that it would not occupy the Republics of Luhansk or Donetsk (a position that, as known, was eventually reversed). The relations between each client – i.e., the separatist region – and the Russian patron are also far from being homogenous: while some of these states have at times expressed a demand to territorially rejoin with Russia (essentially, a repetition of the “Crimean scenario”), others have clearly voiced a desire for independence. 

## An overview of the Dossier contributions 

By patronising and instrumentalising de facto states, the Kremlin has indeed exerted influence in its ‘near abroad’, often as a response to former USSR countries’ desire to exit Moscow’s orbit in favor of improved relations with the West. However, now that the confrontation between Russia and the West over Ukraine has reached unprecedented heights, doubts have been raised about Moscow’s actual capability and willingness to invest in economic and political support for de facto states. Moscow’s “ distraction” – i.e., its massive military and political investment in the Ukraine war – was often cited as a reason for its inaction during the 2023 clashes between Armenia and Azerbaijan. 

To shed some light on the topic, this ISPI Dossier has gathered contributions on the future of Russia-backed separatism. First, Ana Maria Albulescu provides an overview of Russia’s support for breakaway regions in post-Soviet countries, highlighting both the analogies and the specificities in Moscow’s approach. Shorena Nikoleishvili and Toni Selkälä focus on Georgia’s breakaway region of Abkhazia, making the case that Sukhumi’s de facto independence is increasingly at risk. Their contribution offers a valuable context for understanding the clashes between the so-called opposition and the de facto government in Abkhazia currently unfolding at the time of writing. Olesya Vartanyan addresses the case of South Ossetia, suggesting that the fate of the secessionist state will be heavily determined by the trajectory of Russo-Georgian relations. Finally, Giorgio Comai discusses Moldova’s breakaway region of Transnistria, where the status quo between Chișinău’s central government and the secessionist republic may soon be shaken.
